column2: The experience of pleasure and pain, arising from dharma and adharma, brings about place and the like; the creature obtains place and so on in order to enjoy them.
The king said: "O Brahmin, he who exists says 'I am'; how can this not be said? The word 'I' is no fault when applied to the self, O twice-born."
The Brahmin said: "The word 'I' is a fault when applied to the non-self, not to the Self; the notion of self in the non-self, or the word for it, marks delusion.
When the one Person abides in all bodies, then the words 'Who are you? Who am I?' are fruitless.
You are the king, this is the palanquin, we are the bearers going ahead; and this world is yours — but, O king, that is not truly so.
From a tree comes wood, and from it this palanquin on which you sit. What name of 'tree' remains for what is born, or of 'wood', O king?
The great king, seated on the tree, does not say so, being conscious; nor does anyone address you as 'wood' when you are in the palanquin.
The palanquin is an assembly of wooden parts held in an arrangement; O best of kings, look for the palanquin when it is taken apart.
'Man, woman, cow, horse, elephant, bird, tree' — this is the worldly naming of bodies, to be understood as due to karma.
The tongue says 'I', as do the teeth, lips and palate, O king; but these are not 'I', for all are only causes of the production of speech.
What use are causes? Speech itself says 'I am speech' — yet speech is not 'I', so this claim is false and unfitting.
Since the body of a man, marked by head, anus and the rest, is separate, to what, O king, shall I apply the name 'I'?
If there were another, superior to me, O best of kings, then 'this is I, this is another' could be said.
In the highest truth there is no distinction: not mountain, not animal, not tree. Bodies and their varieties are born of karma.
What in the world is called a king, or the retinue of the king's soldiers — that and the rest, O king, is not truly real.
You are king of all the world, son of your father, enemy of your enemy, husband of your wife, father of your son: what then shall I call you, O king?
Are you this head? Or your belly? Are you the feet and so on? Is this yours, O lord of the earth?
You stand apart from all the limbs. Becoming expert, reflect here, O king, 'Who am I?'" Hearing this, the king spoke to that Brahmin, the Avadhuta, who was Hari.
The king said: "I set out to ask the sage Kapila about the highest good, O Brahmin; you are a portion of the sage Kapila, giving knowledge on earth for my sake. Tell me what is the highest good."
The Brahmin said: "Again you ask what is best; you do not ask about the highest truth. All the other goods, O king, are not the highest.
Having worshipped the gods, one wishes for wealth, sons and a kingdom; what is the good of that, O king?
The union of the discriminating with the Supreme Self is the good; it is not a rite such as a sacrifice, and it needs no material means.
The union of the highest-truth self is held to be the highest truth: One, all-pervading, equal, pure, without qualities, beyond Prakriti.
The Self is free of birth, growth and the like, all-going, imperishable, supreme, made of knowledge, unattached, all-powerful, not bound by quality or class.
I shall tell the dialogue of Nidagha and Ribhu; hear it, O Brahmin. Ribhu, a knower, son of Brahma, had as disciple Nidagha, born of Pulastya.
Nidagha, having gained learning, lived in the city on the bank of the Devika. Ribhu thought of him.

After a divine thousand years Ribhu came to see Nidagha. After the Vaishvadeva offering, having eaten, Nidagha said to his guest: "At the end of the meal contentment arises, imperishable and satisfying."
Ribhu said: "He who has hunger feels contentment, O Brahmin, when he has eaten. I had no hunger; why do you ask about contentment?
Hunger and thirst are properties of the body, not mine, O Brahmin. Since you ask, I say: I am always content.
The Person is all-going and pervading like space; so I am the inner Self. How could this be about coming and going?
I am not one who goes or does not go, nor do I live in one place. You are not other than I, nor am I other than you.
As a house of clay, plastered with clay, becomes firm, so this body is earthy, made of earthy atoms.
I am Ribhu, your teacher, come here to give you wisdom, O Brahmin. I shall go; the highest truth has been told to you.
Know this as one; the whole world has no difference. It is the nature of the Supreme Self, called Vasudeva."
After a thousand years Ribhu went again to that city. He spoke to Nidagha, who was standing alone at the edge of the city: "Why do you stand apart, Nidagha?" said Ribhu.
Nidagha said: "O sage, there is a great crowd of people; the king wishes to enter the lovely city; so I stand here."
Ribhu said: "Who here is the king, and who the other people? Tell me, O best of Brahmins, for you know."
Nidagha said: "The one who has mounted the mad elephant, huge as a mountain peak, is the king; the rest are his retinue."
The one below, Brahmin, is the elephant; the one above is the king. Ribhu said: "Which is the elephant here, and which the king?" said Nidagha.
Ribhu climbed up beside Nidagha: "See the example of the mount — as I am above like the king, you are below like the elephant."
Ribhu said to Nidagha: "Which one am I? Tell me." Nidagha bowed and said: "You are my teacher, surely."
Not otherwise is the mind refined by the impressions of duality. Ribhu said to Nidagha: "I came for the knowledge of Brahman; I have shown you the supreme truth, the essence, non-duality."
The Brahmin said: By that teaching Nidagha became devoted to non-duality; he then saw all beings without difference in himself.
He attained liberation by knowledge, and so will you attain liberation. Vishnu is one, the whole, you and I, for he is all-pervading.
As the one sky is seen as yellow, blue and so on, so the Self, to deluded eyes, appears one and many.
Agni said: By the essence of this knowledge the king obtained liberation. Contemplate "Brahman" as the knowledge that is the enemy of the tree of samsara and ignorance.
All prosperous and mighty beings are held to be my portions. Knowing "I alone am the universal form," one is freed.
He who knows the body as the field is called the knower of the field. The knowledge of field and knower of the field is, in my view, true knowledge.
The great elements, ego, intellect and the unmanifest, the ten senses and the one (mind), and the five objects of the senses;
desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, the aggregate, consciousness and firmness: this is the field, briefly stated with its modifications.
Humility, freedom from pretence, non-violence, patience, uprightness, service of the teacher, purity, steadiness, self-control;
dispassion toward objects of the senses, freedom from egotism, reflection on the pain and defect in birth, death, old age and disease;
non-attachment, non-clinging to son, wife, home and the like, and constant evenness of mind in desirable and undesirable events;
unswerving devotion to me through undivided yoga, resort to secluded places, distaste for crowds of people;
constancy in knowledge of the Self and seeing the aim of knowledge of truth: this is declared to be knowledge; what is otherwise is ignorance.
I shall tell what is to be known, by knowing which one tastes immortality: the beginningless supreme Brahman, called "sattva" (being).
It has hands and feet everywhere, eyes, heads and mouths everywhere, hears everywhere in the world, and stands enveloping all.
Shining with the qualities of all senses yet devoid of all senses; unattached yet supporting all; without qualities yet enjoying the qualities.
Outside and inside beings, unmoving and moving; incomprehensible by its subtlety, it is far away and also near.
Undivided in beings yet standing as if divided; to be known as the sustainer of beings, devourer and creator.
The light even of lights, said to be beyond darkness: knowledge, the knowable, the goal of knowledge, seated in the heart of all.
By meditation some see the Self in the self by the self; others by Sankhya, others by karma yoga.
Others, not knowing thus, worship having heard from others; they too quickly cross death, devoted to what they hear.
From sattva arises knowledge; from rajas, greed; from tamas arise negligence, delusion, and ignorance.
He who stays unmoved, thinking "the qualities act," equal toward honour and dishonour, friend and foe, a renouncer, is free of the qualities.
They speak of the imperishable ashvattha tree with roots above and branches below, whose leaves are the Vedas; he who knows it knows the Veda.
There are two creations of beings in this world: divine and demonic. Non-violence, forgiveness and the like belong to the divine endowment of men.
Neither purity nor good conduct arises from the demonic endowment. Since hell comes of them, one should give up the triad of anger, greed and desire.
Sacrifice, austerity and charity are held to be threefold by sattva and the rest. Food that increases life, goodness, strength, health and happiness is sattvic.
Food that is bitter, sharp and dry, causing pain, grief and sickness is rajasic; impure, leftover, rotten or tasteless food is tamasic.
The sacrifice to be performed by rule, without desire for fruit, is sattvic; the sacrifice done for fruit and show is rajasic; and a rite of the other sort is tamasic.
Austerity of the body is that prescribed with faith, mantras and the rules; worship of the gods and the like, and non-violence; austerity of speech is said to be...
...speech that causes no distress, truthful, and the chanting of one's own study; austerity of mind is purity of heart, silence and restraint of anger.
Austerity without desire is sattvic; for fruit or reward it is rajasic; for harm to others it is tamasic. Gift is called sattvic...
...when it is to be given at the right place and time; given for return of favour it is rajasic; given with disrespect and without proper instruction it is called tamasic.
